title: How to Pick the Right Beach in Europe: Sand, Pebbles or Rock
desc: Learn how beach type, exposure and access decide whether a day by the sea works for you.
html:
Europe's beaches are not all the same kind of beach, and choosing the wrong type is the most common way to spoil a day. This guide explains the three main surfaces, what to check before you go, and which type suits which trip.

Sand, pebbles and rock

  • Sand: gentle entry, easy walking barefoot and the best choice for small children. It can get hot at midday and is often the busiest type.
  • Pebbles and shingle: usually clearer water, but the bottom drops quickly and stones are hard on tender feet. Water shoes help a lot.
  • Rock and cove: the best snorkelling and the quietest spots, but they need shoes, some confidence in the water and often a walk to get there.

Check three things before you go

The bottom. Sand slopes gently, pebbles drop fast and rock can hide sea urchins. Exposure. An open bay facing the wind can be rough one day and glassy the next, so check the forecast the evening before. Access. Some of the best coves need a steep path or a boat, and the walk back up is harder in the afternoon heat.

Match the beach to your trip

  • Small children: sand, shallow entry, easy access and a kiosk nearby.
  • Snorkelling: rocky or pebble coves in calm weather.
  • A quiet day: beaches that need a walk, visited early in the morning.
  • Mixed groups: a long beach with both a lively end and a quiet end.

Every beach page on EuroShores lists the surface, access rating and facilities, so you can compare before you commit. Use the Finder to filter for easy, sandy, family-friendly beaches.

title: Beach Day Checklist: What to Pack and What to Skip
desc: A short, practical packing list for a comfortable beach day, from water and shade to cash and offline maps.
html:
A good beach day starts with a short list, not a heavy bag. This checklist covers what makes the biggest difference and what you can leave at home.

Bring

  • Water: more than you think you need. Many quiet coves have no kiosk.
  • Sun protection: a hat, a light shirt and reef-friendly sunscreen.
  • Shade: a pop-up shelter or a large cloth if the beach has no trees or umbrellas.
  • Shoes for stones: water shoes make pebble and rocky entries much easier.
  • Cash: small kiosks, parking attendants and sunbed renters often do not take cards.
  • A rubbish bag: remote beaches often have no bins, so take everything away with you.
  • An offline map: download it before you lose signal on the way in.

Skip

  • Heavy coolers on long walks. Pack light food and a small insulated bag instead.
  • Glass bottles, which are banned on many beaches and dangerous on sand.
  • Drones, loud speakers and open fires unless the local rules clearly allow them.

Timing and safety

Arrive early at popular beaches in July and August, because parking and the best spots go first. Check the wind and swell before entering open bays, and swim near others if there is no lifeguard. Look at the beach flags where they exist and respect them.

Each EuroShores beach page lists parking, sunbeds and food nearby, so you can decide how much to carry.

title: When to Visit Europe's Beaches: Months, Crowds and Water Temperature
desc: Plan around crowds and sea temperature with a month-by-month view of Europe's beach seasons.
html:
The best month for a beach depends on what you want: warm water, fewer people, lower prices or soft light. This guide shows how the seasons differ across Europe's coasts.

Peak summer: July and August

The sea is at its warmest and everything is open, but this is also when parking fills early, sunbeds are priced highest and the most popular beaches are crowded by late morning. Go early or choose a beach that needs a walk.

The sweet spot: June and September

The sea is warm from the summer, the crowds are smaller and the light is softer. For many travellers these are the best months for Mediterranean and Aegean beaches.

Shoulder season: May and October

Southern coasts can be lovely, but the water is cooler and some seasonal kiosks and boat services are closed. Check opening times before you rely on them.

Atlantic versus Mediterranean

  • Atlantic coasts of Portugal, Spain and France stay noticeably colder than the Mediterranean even in summer, and swell can make some beaches unsuitable for casual swimmers.
  • Mediterranean and Aegean seas warm earlier and hold their heat into autumn.
  • Wind matters on open coasts and islands. Sheltered coves are the better choice on windy days.

Each EuroShores beach page lists the best months and the typical water temperature, and the by-month lists group beaches by when they are at their best.

title: Beach Safety Basics: Flags, Currents and Jellyfish
desc: Simple safety rules for swimming at European beaches, from flag colours to rip currents and marine life.
html:
Most beach days go smoothly, and a few simple habits keep it that way. This guide covers the basics of swimming safely at European beaches.

Read the flags

Many lifeguarded beaches use a colour system: green usually means conditions are good, yellow means take care, and red means swimming is not advised or not allowed. Flags and rules vary by country and by beach, so check the signs at the entrance and ask the lifeguard if unsure.

Currents and waves

  • On open Atlantic beaches, strong waves and rip currents are common. If you are caught in one, swim parallel to the shore instead of fighting it, then angle back in.
  • Do not swim alone on exposed beaches, and keep children within arm's reach.
  • Calm Mediterranean coves can still change quickly when the wind rises, so watch the sea as well as the sky.

Marine life

Sea urchins live on rocky bottoms, which is a good reason for water shoes. Jellyfish appear in some seasons and places; look for warning signs and do not touch them, even when washed up. If you are stung, rinse with sea water, remove any visible tentacles carefully and seek help from a lifeguard or pharmacy if the reaction is strong.

Sun and heat

Midday sun is strongest between late morning and mid-afternoon. Use shade, drink water regularly and reapply sunscreen after swimming.

Beach pages on EuroShores note rocky bottoms, open exposure and lifeguard presence where we could confirm them. Rules change, so always follow local signs.

title: Free vs Paid Beaches in Europe: What You Actually Pay For
desc: Understand sunbed fees, parking, boat access and entry charges so you are never surprised at the beach.
html:
In much of Europe the sea and the shoreline are public, so a beach itself is often free to enter. The costs usually come from what surrounds it. This guide explains the common charges so you can plan.

What can cost money

  • Sunbeds and umbrellas: usually the largest cost at developed beaches, with higher prices in July and August. Prices vary widely by country and by beach.
  • Parking: often paid at popular beaches, sometimes by the hour and sometimes with a daily fee. Remote spots may charge informal fees, so ask before you leave the car.
  • Entry and clubs: some private beach clubs and protected areas charge entry or require a booking.
  • Boats and shuttles: some coves are reachable only by boat, with fixed ticket prices.
  • Food and drink: beach bars cost more than village shops.

How to spend less

Bring your own towel and shade, buy water in a village shop, and use the free section of the beach beside the paid area. Visit outside July and August, when prices and crowds both fall. Park farther away and walk if the closest car park is expensive.

Check before you go

Access rules, fees and quotas change from season to season. Some protected beaches limit visitors or need a permit. Always confirm current details with the local tourist office or the official beach page.

EuroShores beach pages list parking and sunbed information where we could verify it.

title: How to Read a Beach Rating on EuroShores
desc: What our beach ratings mean, what we weigh and why a lower score does not always mean a worse day.
html:
Every beach on EuroShores has a rating. This guide explains what it is meant to tell you and what it is not.

What the rating reflects

The score is an editorial judgement based on the beach's setting, water and sand quality, scenery, ease of access and practical facilities, using public sources such as tourism boards and visitor reports. It is meant to help you compare beaches, not to rank them for everyone.

Why a lower score can still suit you

  • A small, quiet cove may score lower for facilities but be perfect if you want peace.
  • A long, easy beach with services may score lower for wildness but be ideal for families.
  • A famous beach may be crowded at peak times even with a high score.

Use the rating with the details

Read the practical information on each page: access, parking, sunbeds, food and best months. Use the Finder to filter for what matters to you, such as family-friendly beaches, free parking or sunbeds.

Corrections welcome

Conditions change and we can be wrong. If you have visited a beach recently, tell us through the Contact page and we will check and update it.

title: Planning a Beach Trip: Choosing a Base and Day Trips
desc: How to pick a base near several beaches and plan easy day trips without wasting time in the car.
html:
The best beach trips are built around a good base, not a long list of beaches. This guide shows how to plan a base and day trips.

Pick a base with choices

Choose a village or town within about 30 to 45 minutes of several beaches, so you can change plans with the wind and the crowds. Look for a base with a shop, a pharmacy and parking.

Plan by wind and crowds

  • Check the forecast each evening and choose a sheltered beach on windy days.
  • Go to popular beaches early, and use the afternoon for quieter ones.
  • Keep one flexible day for weather or rest.

Think about access

Some beaches need a walk, a boat or an early arrival for parking. Add that time to your plan, and carry water, cash and an offline map.

Use the nearby links

Every EuroShores beach page lists other beaches nearby, and the regional pages group beaches by area. Use them to build a day around one stretch of coast instead of driving across a region.

title: Beach Photography Tips: Light, Timing and Crowd-Free Shots
desc: Practical tips for photographing beaches: the best light, simple composition and how to avoid crowds in your frame.
html:
Beaches look their best in the right light, and a few habits make a big difference to your photos, even with a phone. This guide covers light, timing and composition.

Choose the light

  • Early morning and late afternoon: low sun gives warm colour and soft shadows, and the beach is usually emptier.
  • Midday: harsh overhead light flattens colour. Use it for underwater or shade shots instead.
  • Sunset and the hour after: west-facing beaches glow, while east-facing beaches are better at sunrise.

Compose simply

Look for a clear foreground (rocks, shells, footprints or wet sand), a middle subject such as a cove or a boat, and a clean horizon. Keep the horizon straight, and place it in the upper or lower third rather than the middle. Wet sand at low tide can act as a mirror for the sky.

Avoid the crowds

  • Arrive early, or walk a few minutes past the busiest spot.
  • Shoot from a higher angle on a rock or dune to leave people out of the frame.
  • Use a longer focal length to compress the scene and crop out visitors.

Protect your gear

Sand and salt spray damage cameras and phones. Keep gear in a sealed bag, wipe lenses with a clean cloth and avoid changing lenses on the beach. Check tide times so you are never cut off by the sea, and respect drone rules, which many beaches and protected areas restrict.

Each EuroShores beach page lists the best months and the way the beach faces, which helps you plan the light.

title: Reaching Beaches Without a Car: Buses, Ferries and Taxis
desc: How to plan a beach trip by public transport, boat and taxi, and what to check before you rely on them.
html:
You do not always need a car to enjoy European beaches, but you do need a plan. Services thin out in the evening and outside summer, so check before you go.

Buses

Many resort towns run summer bus lines to nearby beaches. Check the first and last service, whether the bus runs daily, and whether tickets are sold on board. Take a photo of the timetable at the stop in case the schedule changes.

Ferries and boats

Some of the best coves are reached only by boat. Water taxis and small boats usually run in season and in good weather, and may be cancelled in strong wind. Agree the return time and price before you leave, and keep some cash for the fare.

Taxis and shared rides

Taxis are useful for the last stretch on rough roads, but ask the driver to confirm a pick-up time because mobile coverage can be weak at remote coves. In some places there are fixed local prices, so ask your accommodation.

Cycling and walking

Coastal paths link neighbouring beaches in many areas. Start early, carry water and check the surface and gradient. Do not underestimate the walk back in the afternoon heat.

Before you rely on it

  • Check services for the exact date, especially outside July and August.
  • Have a backup, such as a taxi number.
  • Download an offline map.

The Access rating on each EuroShores beach page tells you how demanding the approach is, which helps you decide how to travel.

title: Beaches for Families: What to Look for With Young Children
desc: A checklist for choosing a beach that works with babies, toddlers and children: entry, shade, facilities and safety.
html:
A great family beach is less about scenery and more about comfort and safety. Use this checklist when you choose.

Entry and water

  • Gentle slope: shallow, sandy entry lets small children paddle safely.
  • Calm sea: sheltered bays are better than open, windy beaches.
  • Clean bottom: sand is easier than rock or pebbles, and water shoes help on stones.

Comfort

  • Shade: children burn quickly, so bring a tent or umbrella if there is no natural shade.
  • Easy access: a short, flat approach matters with a pushchair and heavy bags.
  • Facilities: toilets, a kiosk and drinking water make a long day easier.

Safety

Choose lifeguarded beaches when you can, and always keep young children within arm's reach. Agree a meeting point with older children, take a photo of what they are wearing, and check warning flags and signs on arrival.

Timing

Go early, when it is cooler and quieter. Plan for a break at midday, and bring snacks and plenty of water.

On EuroShores, use the Finder and tick Family-friendly to list beaches with easy access and sandy shores.

title: Sun Safety at the Beach: A Simple Guide
desc: Simple, practical steps to avoid sunburn and heat problems on a beach day.
html:
The sun is strongest on the coast because water and sand reflect it. A few simple habits keep a beach day comfortable.

Plan around the strongest sun

Midday to mid-afternoon is the hottest period. Swim and walk in the morning and late afternoon, and rest in shade in between.

Cover up

  • Wear a hat, sunglasses and a light long-sleeved shirt.
  • Apply sunscreen generously and reapply after swimming or sweating, following the instructions on the bottle.
  • Pay extra attention to shoulders, nose, ears and the tops of the feet.

Drink and rest

Drink water regularly, even if you are not thirsty. Avoid long periods of alcohol in the heat. Take breaks in the shade.

Know the warning signs

Headache, dizziness, nausea and heavy sweating can signal heat exhaustion. Move to shade, drink water and cool the skin. Seek medical help if symptoms are severe or do not improve.

Children

Keep babies out of direct sun, and use shade, clothing and sunscreen suitable for children. This guide is general information and not medical advice.

title: Snorkelling Basics at Rocky Coves
desc: How to get started with snorkelling at rocky European coves: gear, conditions and simple safety rules.
html:
Rocky coves often have clear water and plenty to see, which makes them good places to try snorkelling. These basics help you start safely.

Gear

  • A mask that seals well on your face, with no strap tightened too hard.
  • A snorkel and, if you like, short fins.
  • Water shoes to protect your feet when you enter over rocks.
  • A rash vest or thin wetsuit if the water is cool.

Choose the conditions

Pick calm days with little wind and swell, and enter from a sheltered side of the cove. Good visibility is usually best in the morning, before the wind rises.

Technique

Breathe slowly through the snorkel and keep your movements gentle. Look down and around, and do not touch or stand on marine life. If water gets in the mask, tilt your head back, press the top of the mask and breathe out through your nose.

Safety

  • Never snorkel alone, and tell someone where you are going.
  • Stay close to shore until you are confident.
  • Watch for boats and use a bright float if boat traffic is possible.
  • Leave sea urchins and jellyfish alone.

EuroShores beach pages note rocky and pebble shores and calm coves, which are good starting points for snorkelling.

title: Leave No Trace on Quiet Beaches: Simple Etiquette
desc: How to enjoy quiet and remote beaches without damaging them: rubbish, dunes, wildlife and respect for locals.
html:
Quiet beaches stay quiet only if visitors look after them. These simple habits protect the places we love.

Take everything with you

Many remote beaches have no bins. Carry a bag for all your rubbish, including food scraps and cigarette ends, and take away any litter you find if you can.

Protect dunes and plants

Stay on marked paths and do not walk on dunes or fragile vegetation. These areas hold the beach together and shelter wildlife.

Respect wildlife

Keep your distance from nesting birds and turtle areas, keep dogs under control where they are allowed, and follow seasonal restrictions and signs.

Be considerate

  • Keep noise low and avoid loud speakers.
  • Park only in designated spots and do not block local roads or access.
  • Do not light fires unless clearly allowed.
  • Do not take shells, stones or sand away from protected areas.

Share carefully

If you post photos of a hidden beach, think about whether the place can handle more visitors. Tag the region rather than the exact spot if it is fragile.

Rules differ by country and beach, so always follow local signs and official guidance.

title: Algarve vs Costa de la Luz: Which Atlantic Coast Suits You
desc: Two Atlantic beach coasts on the same latitude, compared on wind, water temperature, crowds, facilities and style of trip.
html:
The Algarve in southern Portugal and the Costa de la Luz in Andalusia, Spain, face the same ocean and are only a few hours apart by road. They feel very different on the sand, so the right choice depends on what you want from a beach day.

Scenery and beach type

The Algarve is known for golden cliffs, rock stacks and small coves tucked below the headlands, especially around Lagos. The Costa de la Luz is mostly long, open sandy beaches backed by dunes and pine woods, with much more space per person.

Wind and water

Both coasts have Atlantic water that is cooler than the Mediterranean, even in summer. The Algarve coves are often more sheltered, so they suit relaxed swimming. The Costa de la Luz can get a strong easterly wind called the levante, which is excellent for kitesurfing near Tarifa but tiring for sunbathing. Check the forecast the evening before.

Crowds and facilities

The Algarve is busier in July and August, with more developed resorts, restaurants and sunbed rental close to the main beaches, and parking can fill early. The Costa de la Luz is generally quieter and less built up, with simple beach bars called chiringuitos and fewer big resorts, so it suits people who like space more than services.

Which should you choose

Choose the Algarve for small coves, boat trips and easy access to services, and for a first trip to the Atlantic coast. Choose the Costa de la Luz for long walks on empty sand, a more local atmosphere, wind sports and a quieter day, and plan around the wind. Both are best in June and September, when the sea is warm enough and the crowds are smaller.

title: Mallorca vs Menorca: Which Balearic Island for Beaches
desc: A practical comparison of Mallorca and Menorca for beaches: variety, crowds, access, walking and the best time to go.
html:
Mallorca and Menorca are both Spanish Balearic islands with clear Mediterranean water, but they offer different kinds of beach holiday. One is large and varied, the other smaller and quieter.

Size and variety

Mallorca is the larger island, with long sandy bays, small rocky coves, a dramatic mountain coast in the north west and plenty of resorts. That variety makes it easy to find a beach for any mood, but the busiest ones get crowded in summer. Menorca is smaller and calmer, known for pale sand coves on the south coast and a more protected, rural feel.

Access and walking

Many of Menorca best known coves are reached on foot from a car park, sometimes through pine woods, and some car parks fill early or have limited places in high season. Mallorca has more beaches you can drive straight to, but its wildest coves also need a walk or a boat. Wear proper shoes on rocky paths and carry water.

Crowds and prices

Mallorca receives far more visitors, and prices for accommodation and food are usually higher in the busiest areas. Menorca is generally quieter and slower, although the most photographed coves still fill by midday in July and August.

Which should you choose

Choose Mallorca for variety, nightlife options, easy transport and a mix of beach and sightseeing. Choose Menorca for quiet coves, walking and a slower pace, and book accommodation and a hire car early. On either island, arrive at popular coves before mid morning or visit in late May, June or September.

title: Croatia vs Montenegro: Choosing an Adriatic Beach Trip
desc: Croatia and Montenegro compared for beaches: pebbles, islands, water clarity, transport, facilities and costs.
html:
Croatia and Montenegro share the same Adriatic sea and sit close together, yet they suit different travellers. Both have beautiful water, but the beach style, transport and cost can differ a lot.

Beach type

Croatia is known for pebble and shingle beaches, rocky platforms for swimming and many small islands, which give very clear water but need water shoes. Montenegro has a mix of pebble and sandy beaches along a shorter coast, with some pink tinted sand and long stretches near Ulcinj, plus scenic bays around Budva and Kotor.

Islands and transport

Croatia has many islands linked by ferries, so island hopping is a big part of a trip, and the car and ferry planning takes time. Montenegro is compact and easy to cover by car in a day, but public transport to beaches is more limited, so most visitors hire a car or use taxis.

Facilities and costs

Croatia has more developed facilities in popular places, and prices in the busiest towns can be high in July and August. Montenegro has often been cheaper for food and accommodation, though some beaches are crowded, built up or have paid sunbeds that cover most of the sand. Rules and prices change every year, so confirm locally.

Which should you choose

Choose Croatia for island hopping, clear water, sailing and well organised travel. Choose Montenegro for a compact trip, a mix of sandy and pebble beaches and generally lower costs, and be prepared for more variable facilities. For both, the shoulder months of June and September are warm and calmer than August.

title: Greek Islands Compared: Ionian, Cyclades and Crete Beaches
desc: How the Ionian islands, the Cyclades and Crete differ for beaches: wind, scenery, sand, season length and crowds.
html:
Greece has thousands of beaches across several island groups, and the group you choose changes the whole trip. Here are three of the most popular, compared simply.

Ionian islands

The Ionian islands on the west side, including Corfu, Kefalonia, Zakynthos and Lefkada, are greener and have turquoise water, white pebble beaches and dramatic cliffs. They tend to be calmer in summer than the Aegean and have a slightly wetter climate, which keeps the landscape green. Some of the most famous beaches here are reached by boat or a steep path.

Cyclades

The Cyclades, such as Milos, Naxos and Paros, have whitewashed villages, dry landscapes and a very bright look. Summer brings a strong northerly wind called the meltemi, especially in July and August, which can make exposed beaches rough, so choose a sheltered side of the island. Sandy beaches are easy to find on Naxos and Paros.

Crete

Crete is a large island with a long coastline, big sandy bays, pink sand at Elafonissi and gorge beaches on the south coast. It has one of the longest swim seasons in Greece, from late spring into October, and a wide range of facilities. Distances are long, so plan your drives.

Which should you choose

Choose the Ionian islands for scenery, turquoise water and calmer conditions, the Cyclades for whitewashed villages and sheltered coves with careful wind planning, and Crete for variety and a long season. Wherever you go, the best months are usually June and September, when the water is warm and the crowds are smaller.

title: Blue Flag vs Bathing Water Quality: How to Check a Beach
desc: What the Blue Flag award and the official bathing water classification mean, and how to check a beach before you swim.
html:
Before you pick a beach, it helps to know how clean the water is. Two things come up again and again: the Blue Flag award and the official bathing water classification. They are related but they are not the same, and neither tells you everything.

What Blue Flag means

Blue Flag is an annual award given to beaches and marinas that meet a set of criteria. Water quality is one of them, alongside safety, services, environmental information and management. A beach can lose the flag during a season if it stops meeting the criteria. Many excellent beaches have no Blue Flag simply because the local authority never applied, so no flag does not mean a beach is unsafe.

What the official bathing water classification means

In the European Union, countries monitor designated bathing waters during the swimming season and report the results. Each site is classified as excellent, good, sufficient or poor, based on bacteria levels measured over several seasons. A poor classification means local authorities must warn the public and take action. These results are published by the European Environment Agency and by national and regional authorities.

How to check a beach before you go

Search for the beach on the Blue Flag website to see whether it holds the award this year. Then look for the latest classification in the European Environment Agency bathing water report or on the website of the local or regional authority, which often publishes more recent results than the Europe wide summary. Classifications change from year to year, so always check the current season rather than an old article.

Check on the day

Water quality can change after heavy rain, when runoff may carry pollution to the sea for a day or two. Look for notice boards at the beach entrance, which show warnings or bans, and obey flags and signs. If the water looks cloudy, smells unusual or has visible scum, choose another beach nearby.

A simple rule

Use Blue Flag and the official classification as a guide, not a guarantee. A Blue Flag with an excellent classification is a good sign. A beach with no flag but an excellent classification can still be a fine place to swim. If you are travelling with young children or anyone who is vulnerable, take extra care and check the latest local information.

Each beach page on EuroShores links to the official sources so you can check the current status before you go.

Plan the busiest beaches for June or September rather than July and August. The sea is usually still warm, the crowds are smaller and parking is easier.
